newsitem.title: GERMANY: Daimler's Cordes to pay fine for results remarks.
newsitem.headline: Daimler's Cordes to pay fine for results remarks.

text.p: Daimler-Benz AG management board member Eckhard Cordes will pay a fine for revealing a rough estimate of 1996 financial results, but maintains he did not break securities trading regulations, Daimler said on Friday.

Stuttgart prosecutors had been investigating Cordes for allegedly breaking German insider trading laws when in March he provided a small group of journalists with a prediction of 1996 profit figures which had not yet been made public.
But prosecutors said on Friday that they would drop their investigation if Cordes paid a fine -- an offer Cordes accepted.
"He has accepted a proposal to pay a fine and have the investigation dropped," a Daimler spokesman said. "But he is convinced he did not break any laws."
Daimler officials and the prosecutors' office did not provide an exact amount for the fine, saying only it would be between 10,000 and 100,000 marks.

The Federal Securities Supervision Authority, or BAWe, originally filed a complaint against Cordes and questioned whether the profit disclosure should have come via a so-called "ad-hoc" electronic transmission, which German law requires for potentially market-moving information.
Failure to report via the "ad-hoc" route has sometimes constituted a violation of Germany's insider trading rules.

The investigation centred on comments Cordes made to a small group of journalists at the Geneva car show, where he said the company would report net profit of more than two billion marks for the 1996 business year.

The profit forecast, which he made a month before the company's press conference on the 1996 results, was well above analysts' expectations and Daimler's share price rose by more than 3.5 percent the next day.
Daimler went on to report group net income of 2.8 billion marks for 1996.

A spokesman for Daimler, Germany's largest company, said Cordes was convinced he had done nothing wrong, but that he would pay a fine in order to have the investigation halted and spare himself and the company public legal proceedings.
German law allows prosecutors to drop a probe in return for a fine if they believe guilt is hard to prove or negligible. It also has stringent rules about disclosing market-sensitive information.

Cordes, who has been a member of the management board since 1996, stressed to journalists at the car show that Daimler was still working on its financial books for 1996 and the remarks did not amount to a violation of the "ad-hoc" announcement rule, a Daimler spokesman said.
Daimler also said that the prosecutors' investigation never accused Cordes of profiting from insider knowledge in securities trading.
"The prosecutors' office believes there is only a negligible amount of guilt and ultimately, no damage was done," a prosecutors' office spokesman said.
